issues.legal_issue: A municipal authority cannot use subordinate bye-laws to determine property-tax rateable value by a unit-area formula based on property characteristics and value when the governing statute defines rateable value by the rent the property might reasonably be expected to fetch.
material_facts: The governing statute defined rateable value for assessable land and buildings by reference to annual rent reasonably expected from letting the property, subject to a specified deduction.
The impugned bye-laws used a unit-area method that applied assigned values and factors, including area, use, occupancy and age, rather than determining the rent the property could reasonably fetch.

The statute authorized bye-laws on matters relating to taxation under the Act, but the unit-area method was introduced without amending the statutory definition and method of determining rateable value.
issues.conclusion: The unit-area bye-laws were ultra vires the governing statute because they substituted a property-value method for the statutory annual-rent method.
issues.legal_principle: Rateable value under a statutory formula based on the rent at which property might reasonably be expected to let must reflect the rent realizable by the landlord, not the value of the property. The test is the rent the property could lawfully fetch from a hypothetical tenant. Where property is let, actual rent may guide the assessment unless material shows that a different reasonable rent applies; for self-occupied or vacant property, comparable rents may be relevant. Subordinate bye-laws must remain consistent with the parent statute and cannot replace its prescribed basis of assessment. The Court relied on The Corporation of Calcutta v. Smt. Padma Debi, The Guntur Municipal Council v. The Guntur Town Rate Payers’ Association, Dewan Daulat Rai Kapoor v. New Delhi Municipal Council, Indian Automobiles Ltd. v. Calcutta Municipal Corporation, State Trading Corporation v. New Delhi Municipal Council, Government Servant Cooperative House Building Society Ltd. v. Union of India, and Mehrasons Jewellers Private Limited; it applied Sections 2(42), 63(1) and 388(1)(A)(9) of the New Delhi Municipal Council Act, 1994.

predicates.municipal_tax_bye_law_validity_challenge: A party challenges the validity of a subordinate rule used to assess municipal property tax.
predicates.statute_requires_expected_rent: The governing statute requires rateable value to be based on the rent the property might reasonably be expected to fetch from year to year.
predicates.bye_law_uses_property_value_instead_of_e: The subordinate rule assesses value using property characteristics or assigned area values instead of determining the rent the property might reasonably fetch.

issues.definition: If a municipal tax bye-law validity challenge concerns a statute requiring expected rent and a bye-law instead uses property value, the bye-law is ultra vires.

issues.legal_issue: Assessments already paid under invalidated property-tax bye-laws may be left undisturbed for assessees who paid them and were not the original petitioners challenging the bye-laws.
material_facts: The bye-laws had been applied for several years before they were invalidated by the High Court.
The Court was told that about 95% of assessees had accepted the bye-laws and had paid tax on their basis, including through self-assessment under an interim order.
The High Court had directed reassessment, but the Court considered it inappropriate to reopen assessments for assessees who had paid under the bye-laws.
The Court excluded the assessees who had been writ petitioners in the High Court, for whom the High Court’s direction continued to apply.
issues.conclusion: In exercise of its power under Article 142, the Court directed that assessments under the invalidated bye-laws not be reopened for assessees who had paid the tax under them, except the original writ petitioners, whose cases remained governed by the High Court’s direction.
issues.legal_principle: Article 142 of the Constitution permits the Court, in the circumstances of a case, to make an order necessary to do complete justice. The Court used that power to avoid reopening assessments paid under the bye-laws while preserving the relief granted to the assessees who had challenged them in the High Court.

rule.if: appeal_from_invalidation_of_tax_bye_laws and assessment_made_under_invalidated_bye_law and tax_paid_under_assessment and not original_high_court_petitioner

predicates.appeal_from_invalidation_of_tax_bye_laws: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a decision invalidating subordinate rules used to assess municipal property tax.
predicates.assessment_made_under_invalidated_bye_la: An assessee's property-tax assessment was made under the subordinate rules later invalidated.
predicates.tax_paid_under_assessment: The assessee paid the tax assessed under those rules.
predicates.original_high_court_petitioner: The assessee was among the petitioners who originally challenged the rules in the High Court.

issues.definition: When an assessee paid an assessment made under invalidated tax rules and was not an original High Court petitioner, the assessment is not reopened.
